cards.front: What character marks something as an annotation rather than a call or member access?
cards.extra: It appears directly before the annotation type, as in @Override. The compiler reads the name after it as an annotation type, which is why annotations and interfaces share a namespace.

cards.front: In @SuppressWarnings("unchecked"), the element name value is missing. Why is that legal?
cards.back: With a single element named value, the name can be omitted
cards.extra: Writing @SuppressWarnings(value = "unchecked") is equivalent. The shorthand is only for value; any other element name must always be written.

cards.front: When may an annotation be written without parentheses?
cards.extra: Hence @Override and @Deprecated appear bare. The moment an element exists you need @Name(...), even if you supply no value.

cards.front: How does an annotation type declaration begin?
cards.extra: It looks like an interface whose keyword is interface with a leading at sign. Its body holds element declarations that resemble methods and may have default values. @ reads as 'AT', i.e. annotation type.

cards.front: Where must you annotate an annotation type's own definition to get it into Javadoc?
cards.extra: By default annotations on program elements are omitted from generated documentation. Putting @Documented on the annotation type tells javadoc to publish them.

cards.front: Which three java.lang annotations are used by the language and compiler?
cards.extra: They are predefined in every JDK. @Override and @SuppressWarnings steer compiler checks, @Deprecated both warns and documents.

cards.front: What does @Override do when the marked method does not actually override anything?
cards.extra: Using it is optional but catching typos in the method name or signature. Without it, a misspelt override silently becomes a new method in the subclass.

cards.front: Which @Deprecated attribute, added in Java SE 9, marks that the element will be removed in future?
cards.extra: The companion compiler warning category is removal. When an element is deprecated you should also document it with the Javadoc tag @deprecated.

cards.front: Which four warning categories can @SuppressWarnings name?
cards.extra: The array form suppresses several at once: @SuppressWarnings({"unchecked", "deprecation"}). The unchecked warnings arise when mixing with pre-generics legacy code.

cards.front: What does @SafeVarargs assert about a method or constructor?
cards.back: Its varargs body is safe, so no unchecked varargs warning
cards.extra: Applied to a generic varargs method you promise not to store arbitrary types into the array. Java suppresses the heap-pollution warning it would otherwise report at the call site.

cards.front: Which Java SE release introduced @FunctionalInterface?
cards.extra: It marks a type declaration as intended to be a functional interface, meaning one abstract method. It is documentation plus a compiler check against accidental extra abstract methods.

cards.front: RetentionPolicy.SOURCE keeps an annotation where?
cards.back: Source level only - the compiler ignores it
cards.extra: The annotation is available while compiling but never recorded in the class file. @Override is typically SOURCE-retained, since only javac needs to see it.

cards.front: RetentionPolicy.CLASS keeps an annotation where?
cards.back: In the class file - the JVM ignores it
cards.extra: This is the default retention when @Retention is not specified. Bytecode tools can read the annotation, but reflection at runtime cannot see it.

cards.front: RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME keeps an annotation where?
cards.extra: Only RUNTIME-retained annotations are visible through reflection, which is why frameworks that inspect annotations at runtime (JPA, Jackson, JUnit) declare it.

cards.front: Which Java SE release made annotations applicable to type uses, not just declarations?
cards.extra: That is a type annotation: usable on new, on casts, on implements clauses and on throws. It lets a pluggable type checker see where a type is used, not only where a variable is declared.

cards.front: What are type annotations used for?
cards.back: Feed pluggable type checkers that run alongside javac
cards.extra: E.g. declare a variable @NonNull String s. A checker module plugged into the compiler then warns when null could flow in. The JDK ships no checker, only the ability to accept one.

cards.front: Which meta-annotation restricts the element kinds an annotation may be applied to?
cards.extra: Its value is one or more ElementType constants: TYPE, FIELD, METHOD, PARAMETER, CONSTRUCTOR, LOCAL_VARIABLE, PACKAGE, MODULE, TYPE_PARAMETER, ANNOTATION_TYPE, TYPE_USE, RECORD_COMPONENT. The compiler rejects an annotation used in the wrong place.

cards.front: Which ElementType value allows an annotation wherever a type is used?
cards.extra: That covers new, casts, implements and throws clauses. TYPE instead means class, interface, enum, annotation or record declarations.

cards.front: What does @Inherited do when a subclass has no annotation of that type?
cards.extra: Inheritance of annotations is off by default, so without it getAnnotation returns null on the subclass. @Inherited applies only to class declarations, never to methods or fields.

cards.front: To make your annotation apply twice on one element, which meta-annotation declares it repeatable?
cards.extra: Its value names the container annotation the compiler generates to hold the repeats. Applying an annotation twice without it is a compile-time error.

cards.front: A repeatable annotation needs a container. What must the container declare?
cards.back: A value element whose type is an array of the repeatable type
cards.extra: E.g. Schedules holds Schedule[] value(). The compiler then wraps repeated @Schedule annotations into one @Schedules automatically.

cards.front: Which AnnotatedElement method returns all repeated annotations at once?
cards.extra: Added in Java SE 8; it scans the container annotation for you. The older getAnnotation(Class) still returns only one and unchanged, so legacy code keeps working.
